paper_b.title: Simultaneous Analysis of Lasso and Dantzig Selector

metadata.description: Both papers analyze L1-based sparse recovery (basis pursuit / LP decoding in Candes-Tao; Lasso and Dantzig selector in Bickel-Ritov-Tsybakov), but they introduce competing theoretical conditions on the design matrix. Candes-Tao formulate the Restricted Isometry Property (delta_S) plus restricted orthogonality (theta_{S,S'}) and prove exact-recovery / robust-recovery theorems under delta_S + theta_S + theta_{S,2S} < 1. Bickel-Ritov-Tsybakov instead introduce the weaker Restricted Eigenvalue (RE) assumption tailored to noisy regression and establish prediction / coefficient oracle inequalities for both estimators simultaneously, reducing classical RIP-type conditions (now phi_min versus theta_{m_1,m_2}) to sufficient conditions for RE. The pair is paradigmatic competing frameworks: same underlying problem (L1-recovery of sparse signals from linear observations) attacked with different design-matrix conditions and different proof machinery.

matches.explanation: Paper A poses linear-code decoding (recover f from y = Af + e with sparse e); paper B states fixed-design nonparametric regression Y_i = f(Z_i) + W_i with a finite dictionary expansion. Both define the data-generating model that frames sparse recovery, but with different goals: error correction vs prediction/estimation in regression. Same conceptual role (problem statement) with substantially different framing — code-decoding with arbitrary sparse corruption versus Gaussian regression with sparse coefficient vector.

Both quantify sparsity by the l_0 count (number of nonzero entries). Paper A uses ||e||_{l_0} <= rho*m for the corruption vector; paper B defines M(beta) = sum I{beta_j != 0}. Same mathematical object (cardinality of support) used in both frameworks as the sparsity index.

The l_0-minimization problem (P_0) is explicitly formulated only in paper A as the combinatorial 'ground truth' that L1 relaxes. Paper B does not state an l_0-minimization counterpart; it works directly with L1-penalized / L1-constrained estimators. Paper-original contribution of Candes-Tao.

Both pairs are L1-based convex programs for sparse recovery. Paper A: basis pursuit (P_1) min ||d||_{l_1} s.t. Fd = tilde y, and the equivalent direct LP decoder (P'_1) min ||y - Ag||_{l_1}. Paper B: Lasso (penalized L1 least squares) and Dantzig selector (min L1 subject to a sup-norm constraint on the score). The Dantzig selector is the closest formal analogue of basis pursuit (also a linear program with an L1 objective), while Lasso shifts the L1 from constraint to penalty for the noisy regression setting. Same conceptual role; different framings between exact/noiseless and noisy/regression.

Paper A makes the LP form of (P'_1) explicit (min 1^T t s.t. -t <= y - Ag <= t). Paper B refers to the Dantzig selector as a linear program but does not extract the standard-form LP reformulation as a separate object. Minor LP-formulation node specific to paper A.

RIP constants delta_S (paper A) versus restricted eigenvalues phi_min(u), phi_max(u) (paper B) both control the spectrum of submatrices F_T^* F_T / Psi_n on small index sets. RIP: (1 - delta_S) <= ||F_T c||^2 / ||c||^2 <= (1 + delta_S). Restricted eigenvalues: phi_min(u) and phi_max(u) are the min/max of x^T Psi_n x / |x|_2^2 over u-sparse x. They quantify the same property (near-isometry on sparse subsets) but in different normalizations and not packed into a single delta_S. Conceptually exact, formally analogous due to the asymmetric phi_min vs phi_max parametrization in paper B.

Both define a restricted-orthogonality / restricted-correlation constant: paper A's theta_{S,S'} bounds |<F_T c, F_{T'} c'>| <= theta_{S,S'} ||c|| ||c'|| over disjoint S- and S'-sparse subsets; paper B's theta_{m_1,m_2} is the maximum of (c_1^T X_{I_1}^T X_{I_2} c_2) / (n |c_1|_2 |c_2|_2) over disjoint I_1, I_2. After the 1/n normalization (which BRT use because Psi_n = X^T X / n while CT use isometric F), these are the same object. Paper B explicitly cites paper A's restricted-orthogonality constant as the model for theta_{m_1,m_2}.

Paper A's column-norm characterization of delta_1 has no separate counterpart in paper B; paper B encodes column normalization through ||f_j||_n directly without an analogue equation. Auxiliary observation specific to paper A's setup.

Paper A's quantitative comparison theta_{S,S'} <= delta_{S+S'} <= theta_{S,S'} + max(delta_S, delta_{S'}) ties the RIP and ROP constants together. Paper B defines phi_min, phi_max and theta_{m_1,m_2} as separate quantities and does not derive a comparison lemma between them — instead paper B's Lemma 4.1 derives RE constants from combinations of phi_min, phi_max, and theta_{m_1,m_2}. Paper-A-original technical lemma.

Paper A's uniqueness lemma 'delta_{2S} < 1 implies sparse representations are unique' is a noiseless identifiability result for the (P_0) problem. Paper B's noisy regression setting has no analogous uniqueness statement; it instead directly proves stochastic oracle inequalities for the L1-regularized estimators.

Both are the central recovery / estimation theorems for L1-minimization. Paper A's Theorem 1.3 says: under delta_S + theta_{S,S} + theta_{S,2S} < 1, basis pursuit (P_1) exactly recovers any S-sparse signal in the noiseless setting. Paper B's Theorem 5 says: under RE(s,3), Lasso achieves explicit l_1, l_2 prediction, and l_p coefficient bounds in the noisy linear model. Same conceptual role (main L1-recovery guarantee for the L1-penalized / constrained estimator) with different design conditions (RIP+ROP vs RE) and different conclusions (exact recovery vs near-oracle rate).

Paper A's Theorem 1.4 (LP decoder (P'_1) recovers f exactly under sparse corruption) corresponds to paper B's Theorem 4 (Dantzig selector achieves l_1, l_2 prediction, and l_p coefficient bounds). Both are recovery theorems for the L1-constrained / LP estimator; CT's is exact recovery in the noiseless adversarial-corruption setting, BRT's is high-probability oracle bounds in the Gaussian-noise regression model. Same conceptual theorem template, different competing conditions and noise models.

Paper A's Gaussian-matrix analysis (verifying the RIP+ROP main hypothesis with overwhelming probability via Marchenko-Pastur and Ledoux concentration) is a substantial section unique to paper A. Paper B works under the abstract RE assumption and only briefly notes that random designs satisfy it; there is no analogous concentration-based verification in paper B's nodes.

The dual-certificate construction (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 with their iterative l_2 / l_infinity refinement) is paper A's central technical machinery for proving exact recovery via duality. Paper B's proof technique is fundamentally different: it manipulates the optimality / KKT conditions of Lasso/Dantzig and uses cone inequalities + RE directly, never constructing a dual certificate. This is the heart of the 'competing frameworks' relation.

Both sides are the proofs of the main L1-recovery / estimation theorems for the L1-minimizer. CT's PP2.4 proves Theorem 1.3 (exact recovery via basis pursuit) via duality: take a dual certificate w from Lemma 2.2 with <w,v_j> = sgn(c_j) on T and |<w,v_j>| < 1 off T, compare ||d||_{l_1} with ||c||_{l_1} via w, force d_j = 0 off T, then conclude d = c. BRT's three core proofs PP4.7 (Theorem 3, Lasso oracle), PP4.9 (Theorem 4, Dantzig coefficient bounds), PP4.10 (Theorem 5, Lasso coefficient bounds) all share the same cone-inequality + RE machinery applied to the Lasso/Dantzig optimality conditions, with no dual certificate. One-to-many analogy reflecting that CT has one unified proof technique while BRT splits the analysis across two estimators (and a separate Lasso oracle proof) — but the underlying conceptual step (translate optimality + design-matrix hypothesis into the final L1 / l_2 estimation bound) is the same.
Auxiliary remark on possibly improving CT's main hypothesis; no BRT analogue.
Proof of the theta-delta comparison lemma (LP2.1) — paper-A-internal and has no BRT analogue (BRT has different structural lemmas).

Algorithmic counterparts: CT's LP decoder (solve min 1^T t s.t. -t <= y - Ag <= t) versus BRT's two estimators — Lasso (penalized convex program) and Dantzig selector (LP min |beta|_1 s.t. sup-norm constraint). All are L1-based convex programs / LPs for sparse recovery; the Dantzig selector is the most direct algorithmic analogue (also an LP), while Lasso is its penalized cousin.

Both papers establish near-oracle reconstruction rates for non-exactly-sparse signals. CT's Section 5 (Theorem 5.1) bounds ||alpha - alpha^#|| <= C(K/lambda)^{-(s-1/2)} for compressible signals (power-law decay class F_s(B)), under UUP and ERP. BRT's Section 5 establishes Lasso and Dantzig sparsity oracle inequalities of the form ||hat f - f||_n^2 <= (1+eps) inf_{beta} {||f_beta - f||_n^2 + sigma^2 M(beta) log M / n} under the weak sparsity property. Same conceptual role (going beyond exact sparse recovery to handle compressible / approximately-sparse signals) with different formalisms — CT uses oversampling-factor-based UUP/ERP, BRT uses the weak-sparsity definition and oracle-inequality framing.
Numerical experiments (CT Section 4) for (P'_1) recovery have no counterpart in BRT (theory-only paper).
Open problems on tightening the Gaussian-matrix recovery threshold and finite-alphabet extensions are CT-specific.

Paper B's empirical norm ||g||_n and Gram matrix Psi_n = X^T X / n are basic regression-setup definitions (and are essentially the empirical-design counterparts of CT's inner products on H), but they are nondiagonal infrastructural definitions without a direct CT-side counterpart node.

The Restricted Eigenvalue assumptions RE(s,c_0) and RE(s,m,c_0) are the central novel contributions of BRT, designed specifically to be weaker than CT's RIP-type conditions while still being strong enough for Lasso/Dantzig oracle inequalities. They have no direct CT counterpart; BRT motivate them precisely as a relaxation of CT's delta_S + theta + theta hypothesis.

Assumptions 1-5 of BRT are sufficient conditions (in terms of phi_min, phi_max, theta_{m_1,m_2}) implying the RE assumption. They build on CT-style restricted-isometry / restricted-orthogonality quantities, but the bridge lemmas (tying them to RE) and their statements as separate assumptions are paper-B-original. No CT counterpart.
The annihilator reduction (FA = 0 reduces decoding to sparse recovery) is paper-A-specific; paper B does not need this reduction since it works in the regression formulation directly.

BRT's KKT consequence that the Lasso solution automatically satisfies the Dantzig constraint is the bridge between the two BRT estimators. CT studies only the L1-minimization (basis pursuit / LP decoder) so this bridge has no analogue.

BRT's c_0 cone inequality |D_{J_0^c}|_1 <= c_0 |D_{J_0}|_1 is a structural fact about the Lasso/Dantzig residual. CT's proofs work via dual certificates, not cone inequalities, so no direct counterpart.

Lemma 4.1 (restricted positive definiteness) is paper-B-original — the bridge from CT-style phi_min/phi_max/theta quantities to the RE assumption. Its role is precisely to translate the CT framework into the weaker BRT framework.

Lasso oracle inequality on event A (Lemma B.1), Dantzig cone-and-residual control (Lemma B.2), and the Lasso cone corollary (B.1) are the noisy-regression-specific technical lemmas of BRT. CT's noiseless setting has no analogous probabilistic event-based lemma.

Theorems 1 and 2 (approximate equivalence between Lasso and Dantzig prediction losses) are central paper-B contributions: they tie the two estimators quantitatively, showing |||hat f_D - f||_n^2 - ||hat f_L - f||_n^2| is small (up to oracle rate). CT studies only one estimator (basis pursuit / LP decoder) and has no Lasso-vs-Dantzig comparison theorem.
Theorem 6 is the uniform-over-Lambda variant of Theorem 4; paper-B-internal refinement with no CT counterpart.

External-origin results (Marchenko-Pastur eigenvalue limits, Ledoux Gaussian concentration) are cited tools used only in CT's Gaussian-matrix verification. Per the v2 origin-aware filtering rule, external nodes are not aligned against each other unless mutually cited; BRT does not cite these results.

Proof of the noiseless uniqueness lemma LP2.2 (delta_{2S} < 1 ensures uniqueness of S-sparse representations). This is a 2-line contradiction argument particular to the noiseless identifiability question; BRT has no analogous noiseless uniqueness proof.

Proof of BRT's Lemma 4.1 (restricted positive definiteness via block partition + geometric tail summation) — the bridge translating phi_min/phi_max/theta into RE constants. Paper-B-original technique with no CT counterpart.

Proofs of the BRT noisy-regression core technical lemmas (Lasso oracle inequality on event A, Dantzig cone+residual control, Lasso cone corollary). They are based on probabilistic Gaussian-tail events, KKT-style optimality manipulation, and direct algebraic cone derivations — entirely distinct from CT's dual-certificate machinery.

Proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 (approximate equivalence Lasso vs Dantzig prediction losses). These are paper-B-internal cross-estimator comparison proofs with no CT analogue; CT studies only one L1 estimator.
Proof of Proposition 1 (Dantzig sparsity oracle inequality under weak sparsity). Paper-B-internal proof bootstrapping Theorem 1 + Theorem 3; no CT counterpart.
